newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Steady market, shipments up.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Steady market, shipments up.

text.p: After taking half the Sri Lankan wheat tender last week, Australia expected to win most of the next major international tender of 250,000 tonnes being let by Pakistan, an Australian Wheat Board spokesman said on Friday.

The Pakistan tender, for white wheat, is designed for Australian or U.S. wheat. "Australia would expect to get most of that. Otherwise it's got to be U.S. white wheat, although U.S. supplies are so tight they may not be in it. Certainly the U.S. would like to get some of that business," he said.
Some merchants were expected to also work some Argentine wheat into the tender, he said.
Turkey, after 400,000 tonnes of wheat, also would be tendering in the coming week, he said.
Australia's sale of 50,000 tonnes to Sri Lankan deal was priced at US$169.25 a tonne c and f, the spokesman confirmed.

The resumption by the U.S. of the six-monthly $2 billion food-for-oil for Iraq could be expected to have oil pumping by mid-December. "So you could expect to see wheat sales take place shortly thereafter," he also said.
Australia would definitely be after that market, traditionally one of the country's largest, he said.
The Australian harvest was picking up, with AWB shipments at 1.7 million tonnes in the period from the start of October to the end of November, he said.
"(This is) our biggest start to the season since 1989. We're off to a flying start," he said.

The AWB announced during the past week that New South Wales growers had almost reached half-way mark in harvesting a near-record crop with 3.5 million tonnes now received into the system from an expected seven million tonne crop.

A flurry of Australian barley export sales are also beginning to go through, with unconfirmed reports of up to 150,000 tonnes of barley set for January delivery to Saudi Arabia at up to US$133.00 a tonne FOB.
The sales are mainly from Western Australia and South Australia, with more sales in the pipeline, market sources said.
Prices for cash wheat and futures remained steady in a quiet domestic market last week influenced by holidays in the U.S.

Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders (NEAT) said cash prices finished the week where they opened, with Prime Hard wheat delivered silo at about A$160.00 a tonne and other grades in line with this and with the AWB pool price.
The next AWB estimated pool price, to be announced Monday, was expected to be steady, he said.
Mitchell also said the harvest was progressing well with slight lack of protein emerging as the harvest progressed south in NSW but with yields good.
Guy Allen of GrainCorp said farmer selling had come to a standstill as hoped-for higher prices remained steady. But the harvest was progressing well with quality good, he said.
Over the past week, fundamentally steady AWB indicator prices for ASW in the main centres ranged from a A$4.00 decline in Brisbane to a A$5.00 gain in Melbourne.
Steady futures prices over the week edged back by about 50 cents a tonne for near-term contracts and rose by about A$1.00 a tonne for distant contracts.
